title: The Spring Cash Gap: Why Gearing Up for Your Busiest Quarter Drains Cash Before It Delivers Any
linkedin:
Spring starts today. If your business is gearing up for its busiest quarter, the cash to fund it already left the account, weeks before any of that quarter's revenue shows up.

Stock ordered. Casual staff rostered. Marketing spend committed. All of it necessary, all of it normal, and all of it paid for on terms that rarely match the terms customers get to pay on. A supplier invoice due in 30 days sits next to a customer invoice that will not be collected for 60.

That gap is not a sign anything has gone wrong. It is the structure of trading, and it stretches furthest exactly when volume is ramping up, which is exactly when most owners are too busy to be watching for it.

The costly part is not the gap itself. It is funding it by default, whatever cash reserve, credit card or stretched supplier term happens to be available in the moment, rather than choosing the funding source on purpose, months ahead of time.

A rolling 13-week cash flow forecast turns "we might be tight later this year" into a specific week, a specific shortfall and a specific plan. Once the shape of the gap is visible, the decision gets made calmly in September rather than under pressure in November.

That gap between spending now and getting paid later is completely normal. It is also the part most owners have never actually mapped out week by week, which is exactly how a genuinely profitable quarter ends up feeling like the tightest one of the year.

Honest question: if your busiest few months are just ahead, do you know which week the cash gets tightest, or are you finding that out as it happens?

Spring starts today, and for a lot of owner led businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, that means the busiest trading quarter of the year is already underway on the spending side. Stock gets ordered, casual staff get rostered, and marketing spend gets committed well before any of that season's revenue actually lands in the bank.

This is not a sign anything has gone wrong. It is simply what gearing up for a strong season looks like from the inside. The businesses that get caught out are rarely the ones doing badly. They are the ones doing well enough to be busy, without having mapped out which week the outgoing spend on stock and staff will outpace what is coming in from sales.

A rolling forecast covering the next thirteen weeks shows that gap in advance, week by week, so the choice of how to fund it can be made calmly now rather than discovered under pressure in a few months. The number does not remove the gap. It just means the business gets to choose the terms on which it covers it.
